honesty.name: How we know
honesty.like: Every part of this page says where its information comes from.
honesty.text: Not everything on this page was recorded from your code. So each zoom level, and each panel that differs from its zoom level, carries one of these labels, which says how we know what it shows. Every label opens this card.

bit.name: Bit
bit.like: A single light switch: on or off.
bit.text: The smallest piece of information a computer can store. A bit is either on or off, written as 1 or 0. In RAM, or on an SSD, a bit is a tiny electric charge that is either there or not there.

byte.name: Byte
byte.text: A group of 8 [[bit|bits]]. Eight switches can be set in 256 different on/off patterns, so one byte can hold any whole number from 0 to 255. Almost everything in a computer is counted in bytes: file sizes, memory, text.

visual.note: The byte for **)**: switches 32, 8 and 1 are on.

binary.name: Binary
binary.like: Counting with only two digits, 0 and 1.
binary.text: Each of the 8 switches in a byte has a value: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1, from left to right. To read a byte, add up the values of the switches that are on. For the letter **p**: 64 + 32 + 16 = **112**.

utf8.name: UTF-8
utf8.like: A shared dictionary that says which number stands for which character.
utf8.text: A computer can only store numbers, so every character needs an agreed number. UTF-8 is the agreement almost every computer uses today. English letters, digits and common symbols take one [[byte|byte]] each. Other characters take two, three or four bytes. The first 128 numbers match ASCII, an older agreement from the 1960s.

encoding.name: Encoding and decoding
encoding.like: Writing a message in a code, and reading it back.
encoding.text: **Encoding** turns characters into bytes, for example when your editor saves a file. **Decoding** turns bytes back into characters, for example when Python reads your file. Files store text as bytes; Python decodes those bytes into text using [[utf8|UTF-8]]. Once decoded, Python keeps the text as a sequence of characters (a **str**), not as the raw bytes from the file.

newline.name: Newline
newline.like: The Enter key, stored as a character.
newline.text: An invisible character that means “start a new line”. In [[utf8|UTF-8]] it is number 10. Editors don’t show it; they just move down a line. Some Windows editors store it as two bytes, 13 then 10. Some editors don’t add one after the last line. This app always does, so every line of your program ends with one.

token.name: Token
token.text: The smallest meaningful piece of code: a name like **print**, a piece of punctuation like **(**, a piece of text like **"Ada"**. Python’s tokenizer reads your characters one by one and groups them into tokens, the way you read letters and see words.

structure.name: Structure (syntax tree)
structure.like: Grammar: which words belong together, and what role each one plays.
structure.text: After tokenizing, Python works out what your code means and records it as boxes inside boxes. Programmers call it a **syntax tree**, because drawn another way it looks like an upside-down tree. The boxes keep the meaning and drop the punctuation.

code.name: Your steps
code.like: A recipe card: the steps, written down in order.
code.text: Python doesn’t carry out your code as you typed it. First it turns it into small, simple steps, called **bytecode**, and keeps them in [[ram|RAM]]. Your program gets its own list of steps, and so does each function in it. Then [[py|Python itself]] carries out the steps, one at a time.

py.name: Python itself
py.like: The cook: knows how to carry out every kind of recipe step.
py.text: Python’s own program, the **interpreter**. The usual one is called CPython. It is copied into [[ram|RAM]] when Python starts; in this app, it runs inside your browser. Python doesn’t turn your code into [[cpu|CPU]] instructions. It turns it into [[code|steps]], and the interpreter reads each step and does what it says.

frame.name: Frame
frame.like: A desk set up for one job.
frame.text: The workspace Python sets up each time a piece of code runs: its [[stack|plates]], its bookmark saying which step it is on, and its variables. When a function calls another, the caller’s frame waits under the new one. When the code finishes, its frame is cleared away.

disk.name: Disk
disk.like: A pantry: lots of room, keeps everything even when the power is off, but slow to fetch from.
disk.text: Where files live: your documents, and the programs your computer can run. Nothing runs from the disk directly. Programs and data are copied into [[ram|RAM]] first. This app never saves your program to the disk: it keeps it in RAM.

ram.name: RAM
ram.like: The kitchen counter: the workspace. Quick to reach, smaller than the pantry, and wiped clean when the power goes off.
ram.text: Everything a running program uses lives here: its instructions, its data and its [[stack|plates]]. Every [[byte|byte]] of RAM has a number, its **address**, so the [[cpu|CPU]] can find it. For a short program, almost all the RAM it uses goes to [[py|Python itself]].

heap.name: Objects
heap.like: The shelves where the ingredients sit.
heap.text: Every value in Python, such as a number, a piece of text or a function, is an **object**, sitting somewhere in this area of [[ram|RAM]], called the **heap**. An object takes some bytes for its value and some for Python’s bookkeeping. Python makes room for new objects as your program needs them.

stack.name: Plates
stack.like: A stack of plates: you add to the top and take from the top.
stack.text: What Python is holding right now, in the middle of a step. A plate never holds an [[heap|object]] itself, only a label pointing to it: the object’s address in [[ram|RAM]]. Each piece of code that is running, such as a function call, has its own stack of plates. The [[cpu|CPU]] keeps a separate stack of its own, to remember where to come back to after a jump.

none.name: None
none.like: An empty box that means “nothing here”.
none.text: Python’s way of saying “no value”. A function with nothing to give back, such as print, answers with None. There is only one None object in all of Python: every None anywhere is a label pointing to the same one.

cpu.name: CPU
cpu.like: The stove: where every action actually happens.
cpu.text: The CPU carries out instructions: move a number, do arithmetic, compare, jump. It reads them from [[ram|RAM]], through its [[cache|cache]]. Modern CPUs run at billions of clock cycles per second, but one instruction doesn’t necessarily take one cycle: a CPU can work on several instructions at once, and some instructions take many cycles.

reg.name: Registers
reg.like: The burners on the stove: only a few pans fit, and those are what’s cooking this instant.
reg.text: A handful of storage slots inside the [[cpu|CPU]] itself. Every number the CPU works on passes through them. A common kind of CPU, x86-64, has 16 main registers of 8 bytes each.

cache.name: Cache
cache.like: A tray right next to the stove, with copies of what’s used most.
cache.text: Copies of recently used pieces of [[ram|RAM]], kept inside the [[cpu|CPU]] so it doesn’t have to wait for RAM. While a program runs, its busiest parts sit here.

os.name: Operating system
os.like: The restaurant manager, the only one with keys to the doors: to the screen, the disk and the network.
os.text: Programs aren’t allowed to touch the hardware. To read a file from the [[disk|disk]] or show text on the [[screen|screen]], they ask the operating system. Its core, the **kernel**, also decides which program the [[cpu|CPU]] runs next, and gives each program its share of [[ram|RAM]].

terminal.name: Terminal
terminal.like: The order window: you call in what you want, and whatever the kitchen sends out appears there.
terminal.text: A window for talking to programs by typing. You type a command, and the program it names starts. What the program prints reaches the terminal as [[byte|bytes]]; the terminal turns them back into characters and draws them on the [[screen|screen]]. On Windows, you type commands in PowerShell or Command Prompt.

screen.name: Screen
screen.like: The dining room: where the finished dish is finally seen.
screen.text: A grid of tiny dots of light, called **pixels**. Most screens make each pixel’s color from red, green and blue parts. The picture is kept in memory, and the screen redraws it many times a second, often 60.
